title: Word 22 — On Pride
attribution_note: Word 22 of 28 in the collection Short Moral-Instructive Words — see Word 1 for provenance.

sections.heading: The root of pride: not knowing oneself

pairs.en: Pride is a most detestable sin, yet few recognize it in themselves, for it lies hidden deep in the heart. The beginning of pride is ignorance of oneself. This ignorance blinds a man, and so he grows proud. Oh, if a man truly knew himself — knew his poverty, his destitution, and his wretchedness — he would never be proud! But he is all the more wretched for failing to see and know his own poverty and wretchedness. Pride is known by its deeds, as a tree is known by its fruits.
Let us look, then, at what fruits grow from this bitter seed of pride.

sections.heading: The fruits of pride, part one: craving honor, chafing at loss, overreaching

pairs.en: 3) He undertakes tasks beyond his strength, which he cannot accomplish. O man! Why do you lay hold of a burden you cannot carry?

sections.heading: The fruits of pride, part two: meddling and self-praise

pairs.en: 6) He despises and belittles other people: “He is a base man, he is worthless,” and so on. But O man — he is as much a man as you are, for we are all human. He is a sinner, but I think you too will not disown that name for yourself. He has sinned or sins in this matter, and you in another — perhaps even in the very same one. *“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God”* [Romans 3:23].

sections.heading: The fruits of pride, part three: defiance and false credit

pairs.en: 8) Whatever good he possesses, he credits to himself — to his own effort, labor, and intellect — and not to God. O man! What can you call your own, you who came naked from your mother's womb? What can you have, if God, the source of every good thing, does not grant it to you? What can our striving and labor accomplish without the help of Him who alone can do all things, and apart from whom each of us is nothing, like a shadow without a body?

sections.heading: The fruits of pride, part four: intolerance of correction and hardship

pairs.en: 11) In his words and actions he displays a certain haughtiness and ostentation, and the like.

sections.heading: Bitter fruit, bitter seed — and the remedy of humility

pairs.en: The virtue opposed to pride is humility. As detestable and repugnant as pride is, just so pleasing and beloved by God and men is humility. On nothing does the great and exalted God look with such tenderness as on a humble and contrite heart. That is why the Most Holy Theotokos says of herself: *“He has regarded the humility of His handmaiden”* [Luke 1:48]. When pride departs from a man, humility takes up dwelling in him, and the more pride diminishes, the more humility grows, for the one yields its place to the other as its opposite. Darkness withdraws, and light comes in. Darkness is pride; humility is light.
Let us write these words and engrave them deep in our memory, the word of the apostle: *“God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.”* Amen.
